questions.question: A stable patient has one unexpectedly high office blood-pressure reading after rushing to the clinic. What is the best first FNP action?
choices: Diagnose chronic hypertension immediately
Repeat the measurement using correct technique and obtain a reliable pattern of readings
Ignore the result because the patient feels well
Start several medications before clarifying the measurement
questions.explanation: One reading is a snapshot. Correct technique, repeated measurement, and appropriate home or out-of-office data help distinguish sustained hypertension from measurement error, transient elevation, or white-coat effect.

questions.question: Which presentation most strongly suggests hypertensive emergency rather than routine outpatient follow-up?
choices: Elevated BP with new focal weakness and difficulty speaking
Mildly elevated BP after a caffeinated drink with no symptoms
A patient asking how to use a home cuff
Longstanding stable readings with a normal examination
questions.explanation: Marked BP elevation with possible acute neurologic, cardiac, respiratory, renal, aortic, retinal, or pregnancy-related target-organ injury requires emergency evaluation.

questions.question: Why can chronic hypertension contribute to chronic kidney disease?
choices: It permanently improves renal blood flow
Persistent vascular pressure can injure renal arterioles and nephrons
It eliminates sodium retention
It prevents albuminuria
questions.explanation: Chronic pressure-related vascular injury can damage renal microvasculature and nephrons. Kidney disease can then worsen hypertension through altered sodium handling and neurohormonal activation.

questions.question: Before labeling a patient as having resistant hypertension, which step is essential?
choices: Verify adherence, measurement technique, access, interfering substances, and secondary-cause clues
Assume the current medicines are ineffective
Stop all antihypertensives at once
Exclude all lifestyle and access factors
questions.explanation: Apparent resistance may reflect pseudoresistance: incorrect cuff use, white-coat effect, missed doses, cost, NSAIDs or other contributors, high sodium exposure, or an unrecognized secondary cause.

questions.question: Which medication or exposure should be specifically reviewed because it can worsen blood-pressure control?
choices: Frequent nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use
A correctly sized BP cuff
A written home-monitoring log
A follow-up appointment
questions.explanation: NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants, nicotine, alcohol, some hormonal therapies, corticosteroids, and other substances can raise BP or interfere with treatment.

questions.question: What makes lifestyle counseling clinically useful for hypertension management?
choices: It is specific, feasible, and matched to access, culture, function, and patient priorities
It consists only of telling every patient to lose weight
It replaces all reassessment and monitoring
It should avoid asking about food access or sleep
questions.explanation: Lifestyle care is active treatment. It should address realistic nutrition, sodium, activity, sleep, tobacco, alcohol, stress, and access barriers rather than offering vague or stigmatizing advice.

questions.question: A patient with CKD starts a medication that affects renal hemodynamics and later has a creatinine or potassium change. What is the FNP principle?
choices: Interpret the change with volume status, timing, indication, symptoms, and monitoring context
Automatically stop every medication without assessment
Ignore all laboratory changes
Assume kidney disease makes BP management unnecessary
questions.explanation: Kidney and electrolyte changes require context. The correct response may involve reassessment, laboratory follow-up, medication adjustment, or consultation—not an automatic rule applied to every patient.

questions.question: Why must pregnancy status or pregnancy potential be considered in hypertension care?
choices: Pregnancy has no effect on BP assessment or medication safety
Some therapies and BP patterns require pregnancy-specific safety and obstetric coordination
Only postpartum patients need BP assessment
General adult algorithms always apply unchanged in pregnancy
questions.explanation: Hypertension in pregnancy and postpartum warning symptoms require pregnancy-specific evaluation and treatment choices. Medication safety and urgency differ from general adult care.

questions.question: A patient has uncontrolled BP, loud snoring, daytime sleepiness, and obesity. Which contributor deserves focused assessment?
choices: Sleep-disordered breathing
A harmless white-coat effect only
A normal retinal examination
A single missed meal
questions.explanation: Obstructive sleep apnea is a common contributor to difficult BP control and cardiovascular risk. It should be considered within a broader assessment of symptoms and comorbidities.

questions.question: Which follow-up plan best represents FNP-level hypertension care after treatment is started or changed?
choices: Define home monitoring, symptom precautions, relevant laboratory checks, result ownership, and a specific reassessment date
Tell the patient to return only if the medication runs out
Rely on one future office reading without discussion
Avoid discussing adverse effects or affordability
questions.explanation: Safe longitudinal care assigns monitoring and follow-up clearly. It includes readings, symptoms, adverse effects, relevant labs, access, education, and responsibility for reviewing results.
